**Everything the X-24B demonstrated is now done by software, and the one thing that has not moved is the corridor, because the corridor is set by energy rather than by skill.**

A second answer is more radical. **The X-24's entire difficulty was that almost no energy could be added after the approach began.** A booster that lands on its engine answers that by adding energy, and so never attempts an unpowered landing. **Both answers are in service, in the [Boeing X-37][ref_x37] and the [Falcon 9][ref_falcon_9], and they are opposites.**

The cluster subsections after these analytic ones map the field as it currently stands.

### The Flare Is Now a Control Law

Unpowered precision landing is no longer a piloting achievement but a guidance problem with a published solution, for an unpowered reusable launch vehicle in [AL-Bakri and Kluever 2017][research_al_bakri_kluever_2017], for unpowered drones and gyroplanes in [Kim and Tahk 2019][research_kim_tahk_2019] and [Fang et al. 2019][research_fang_2019], for fixed-wing aircraft in flight test in [Woodbury and Valasek 2016][research_woodbury_valasek_2016] and [Sedlmair et al. 2022][research_sedlmair_2022], and for spacecraft in [Lunghi et al. 2015][research_lunghi_2015] and [Robertson 2017][research_robertson_2017], with a review in [Pogosyan and Vereikin 2020][research_pogosyan_vereikin_2020].

**The milestone came thirteen years after the X-24B.** On 15 November 1988 the Soviet orbiter Buran flew one uncrewed orbital mission and landed itself on the runway at Baikonur, unpowered, in a crosswind, with no pilot aboard at any point. **It was the demonstration Manke and Love flew, performed by a machine, at more than fifteen times the weight**, since Buran's dry mass alone was 62 tonnes [Buran][ref_buran] against the X-24B's 8,500 pounds.

**What the automation did not do is widen the corridor.** The bounds derived above are energy bounds and they do not care who is flying. Written out, the touchdown speed is a function

$$
V_\text{td} = F\left(n,\ \frac{W}{S},\ C_{D_0},\ k_i,\ \rho\right)
\tag{72}
$$

in which **there is no term describing the pilot**. An autonomous vehicle arriving too fast still floats, and one arriving too slow still runs out of speed. What automation provides is consistency in hitting the middle of a corridor whose width is set by aerodynamics, in [Bottasso and Montinari 2015][research_bottasso_montinari_2015], [Ye et al. 2015][research_ye_2015], [Zhou et al. 2015][research_zhou_2015], [Ellerbroek et al. 2016][research_ellerbroek_2016], [Ackerman et al. 2017][research_ackerman_2017], [Lee et al. 2017][research_lee_2017], [Lombaerts et al. 2017][research_lombaerts_2017], [Schuet et al. 2017][research_schuet_2017], [Tekles et al. 2017][research_tekles_2017], [Fellah and Guiatni 2019][research_fellah_guiatni_2019], [Gabrys et al. 2019][research_gabrys_2019], [Zaal et al. 2019][research_zaal_2019], [Van Baelen et al. 2020][research_van_baelen_2020], [Campbell et al. 2022][research_campbell_2022], [Kluever 2022][research_kluever_2022], [Yu et al. 2022][research_yu_2022], [Ma and Chen 2023][research_ma_chen_2023], [Altunkaya et al. 2024][research_altunkaya_2024], [Catak et al. 2024][research_catak_2024], [Hsu et al. 2024][research_hsu_2024], [Schieni et al. 2024][research_schieni_2024], [Autenrieb 2025][research_autenrieb_2025], [Sarah et al. 2025][research_sarah_2025], [Yue et al. 2025][research_yue_2025].

### The Other Answer Was to Refuse the Problem

**A propulsively landed booster does not solve the unpowered landing. It declines to have one**, as the powered descent guidance of [Sagliano 2018][research_sagliano_2018], [Wang et al. 2019b][research_wang_2019_2] and [Botelho et al. 2022][research_botelho_2022] and the retropropulsion aerodynamics of [Marwege and Gülhan 2023][research_marwege_gulhan_2023] assume. The propulsive and planetary landing cluster holds the remainder.

The comparison deserves care, because it is a trade and not a victory. The X-24B carried no propellant for a powered approach, only the small landing rockets that [Reed][book_reed_1997] lists among its equipment, and paid for that with a corridor four tenths of a g wide and no second attempt. A booster that lands on its engine carries propellant it could otherwise have spent on payload, and for that it gets a hover, a divert and an abort.

**Which is better depends entirely on what is coming back.** For a stage that is mostly empty tank the propellant is affordable. For a vehicle returning from orbit with a heat shield already sized for the entry, carrying landing propellant through that entry is expensive. That cost is why the winged and lifting vehicles that come back from orbit still land the X-24B's way and the ones that come back from a few minutes of flight do not.

### The Configuration Survived, Uncrewed

The shape is still flying, in India's reusable launch vehicle technology demonstrator, in [Sivan and Pandian 2018][research_sivan_pandian_2018], and in the unpowered approach and landing guidance written for such vehicles, in [Kluever and Neal 2015][research_kluever_neal_2015], [Hameed and Bindu 2021][research_s_hameed_g_r_2021] and [Yao and Xin 2023][research_yao_xin_2023], and it survived in the form the X-24B pointed at and not the X-24A's. **Vehicles of this class are now designed to land themselves on runways**, the capability the two 1975 landings were run to establish. The lifting-body and orbiter clusters below list further examples.

**What did not survive is the pilot in the vehicle**, and with the pilot went most of the reason to care about handling qualities in the way the programme did.

### Computed Drag and a Still-Hard Base

Base and afterbody flows are among the least forgiving things to compute, as large eddy simulation of bluff-body wakes in [Blanchard et al. 2015][research_blanchard_2015] and [Tran et al. 2017a][research_tran_2017_2], hybrid methods in [Schmidt and Breuer 2015][research_schmidt_breuer_2015], nozzle separation in [Yaravintelimath et al. 2016][research_yaravintelimath_2016] and turbulence-model work in [Wu et al. 2017][research_wu_2017] and [Spalart and Garbaruk 2021][research_spalart_garbaruk_2021] show. **The separated region behind a blunt base is unsteady, three-dimensional and sensitive to the approaching boundary layer**, the combination that steady turbulence models handle worst. The Hoerner correlation with a flight-corrected coefficient remains a serviceable engineering answer for the same reason it did in 1975.

### The Physics Migrated to Lorries

**The most active base-drag literature today is not aeronautical**, as the boat tails, deflectors and append devices for heavy vehicles in [khosravi et al 2015][research_khosravi_2015], [Her et al. 2016][research_her_2016], [Lee and Lee 2017][research_lee_lee_2017], [Kim et al. 2020][research_kim_2020], [Gao et al. 2022][research_gao_2022] and [Xu et al. 2022b][research_xu_2022_2] and the platoon studies in [Tadakuma et al. 2016][research_tadakuma_2016] illustrate, and as the road vehicle cluster and the bluff-body share of the base drag cluster below count.

A heavy goods vehicle is a blunt-based body whose drag is dominated by its wake, the X-24's problem in a different medium and at a lower speed. **One of the authors of the lifting-body base-drag analysis also reassessed the aerodynamic design of heavy trucks**, in [Saltzman and Meyer 1999][ref_saltzman_meyer_1999], drawing on coast-down tests of a box-shaped van, a two-axle truck and a tractor-semitrailer, and no statement of the connection could be more direct. Projectile base bleed and boat-tailing belong to the same family.

**The physics travelled because the drag bucket does not care what the body is for.** Base drag falls as forebody drag rises whatever the body, so the factor of three at the optimum is as true of a lorry as of a lifting body.

### Lift Without a Wing, Computed

Aspect ratios near one remain awkward, in [Lian 2011][research_lian_2011], [Rockwell 2011][research_rockwell_2011], [Arivoli and Singh 2016][research_d_singh_2016], [Amin Boukenkoul et al. 2017][research_amin_boukenkoul_2017], [Cao and Tafti 2018][research_cao_tafti_2018], [Obeid et al. 2019][research_obeid_2019], [Okamoto et al. 2019][research_okamoto_2019], [Qi and Wang 2019][research_qi_wang_2019], [Chandra 2020][research_chandra_2020], [Gildersleeve and Amitay 2020][research_gildersleeve_amitay_2020], [Kase et al. 2020][research_kase_2020], [Barrett-Gonzalez and Wolf 2021][research_barrett_gonzalez_wolf_2021], [Chopra and Mittal 2021][research_chopra_mittal_2021], [Lin et al. 2021][research_lin_2021], [Degani 2022][research_degani_2022], [Dutta et al. 2022][research_dutta_2022], [Traub 2023][research_traub_2023], [Syed Abdullah Al Mamun 2024][research__2024], [Jiang et al. 2024][research_jiang_2024], [Verma and Kulkarni 2024][research_verma_kulkarni_2024], [Berci 2025][research_berci_2025], [Eraslan 2025][research_eraslan_2025], [Lampropoulos and Sarris 2025][research_lampropoulos_sarris_2025], [Numerical Investigation of Impinging 2025][research_numerical_investigation_2025], [Degani 2026][research_degani_2026]. **The classical relations still do not describe these shapes**, because their lift comes substantially from crossflow and from vortices shed off sharp edges instead of from circulation in the ordinary sense, which also explains why the article had to take an efficiency factor from a source rather than compute one.

### Handling Qualities Became a Discipline With Numbers

The question of whether a pilot can work with a vehicle is now posed quantitatively, in [Hebbar and Pashilkar 2016][research_hebbar_pashilkar_2016], [Efremov et al. 2020][research_efremov_2020], [Bidinotto et al. 2021][research_bidinotto_2021], [Ivler et al. 2022][research_ivler_2022] and [Lampton et al. 2024][research_lampton_2024], with the rest in the handling qualities cluster below. **The lifting bodies' handling qualities record is part of that literature**, in [Manke et al. 1970][research_john_a_manke_1970], [Kempel and Manke 1974][research_kempel_manke_1974] and [Kempel et al. 1975][research_kempel_1975], not for their shapes but because they were difficult aircraft flown to a standard by people who wrote down what happened.

### What the Gear Sees, Now Measured

The touchdown conditions this article computes at residual path angles are now extracted from the routine flight data of transport aircraft to predict hard landings, in [Ding et al. 2020][research_ding_2020], [Xiangzhang et al. 2024][research_xiangzhang_2024], [Dong et al. 2025][research_dong_2025], [Bansal et al. 2026][research_bansal_2026] and [Chu et al. 2026][research_chu_2026]. **Hard-landing prediction from routine flight data is an established subject, and the distribution of touchdown conditions across a fleet is a measured quantity** where in 1975 it was an estimate.

### What the Survey Shows

**The aerodynamics have not moved.** A truncated base still costs a factor of the square root of three in lift-to-drag ratio, the flare still has a corridor bounded from both ends, and the energy is still spent exactly once.

**What moved is who flies it, and whether the problem is accepted at all.** The X-24B's pilots hit a fifteen-thousand-foot runway from a corridor a few tenths of a g wide, twice, and that was the demonstration. A modern vehicle of that class, such as the [Boeing X-37][ref_x37], lands itself on a runway at the end of every mission. **And a modern booster refuses the problem entirely by carrying the propellant to add energy back**, an option the X-24B did not have and would not have wanted.

### Approach, flare and automatic landing

**The keystone's descendants.** Approach and landing guidance, the flare and its control laws, automatic landing of aircraft and drones, carrier landing, ground effect and the energy of the approach.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Treating the X-24 through its landing gets three things wrong.**

**The vehicles were not landing demonstrators.** They were transonic and low-supersonic research aircraft that happened to land without engines because that is how they were flown. The X-24B reached 1,164 miles an hour, and a great deal of the flight record is about stability and control at speeds that have nothing to do with the approach.

**The base drag analysis is retrospective.** Saltzman, Wang and Iliff published in the 1990s and 2000s, in [Saltzman et al. 1999][research_saltzman_1999], [Saltzman et al. 2002][research_saltzman_2002] and [Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007], drawing on flight data gathered decades earlier. **Nobody sized the X-24B using the factor of three derived above.** The relation explains the vehicle rather than having produced it, and this article should not be read as a reconstruction of the design process.

**The flare corridor is computed from a point-mass energy model**, with a constant load factor and a drag polar that is a parabola. A real flare has neither. The agreement to nine percent is encouraging and is not a validation.

There is a fourth, about attribution. **Two concrete landings do not by themselves settle a design decision** as large as deleting an orbiter's engines. They were one input among many, and the article's account of the causal chain leans on a programme retrospective rather than on the decision record.

## The Source Base

The research literature here is drawn from the NASA Technical Reports Server, from Defense Technical Information Center records reached through their registered identifiers, and from the Crossref index. **The research survey holds 2,851 research records**, counting the survey's own definitions among the References, of which 946 are report primaries, being 33.2 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 1999.** Of the 2,816 dated records, 712 were published before 1976, the period in which the lifting bodies flew, being 25.3 percent, and 1,188 were published in 2015 or later, being 42.2 percent.

**The survey holds 9 records whose titles name the X-24 or its SV-5 designation**, 8 of them report primaries. Most are the programme's own record, from the full-scale tunnel tests of the X-24A to the X-24B's flight test reports.

**This article and the X-23 article share a vehicle family and only a minority of their literature**, because entry mechanics at Mach 25 and unpowered landing at Mach 0.5 are different subjects with different vocabularies.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The reports this article's argument rests on are report primaries under that rule**, among them Larson's landing statistics, the flight-determined lift and drag of Saltzman, Wang and Iliff, Dana and Gentry's account of the approach, and Manke and Love's report of the X-24B programme. **The rule does not reach the journal papers among the foundational sources**, such as Hoerner on base drag and thick trailing edges, so 33.2 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the landing flare | flare, flares, flare out, flared landing, flaring | 37 |
| the trade between forebody drag and base drag | forebody, fore body together with base, afterbody, boattail, boat tail | 2 |
| touchdown sink rate | sink rate, sink rates, sink speed, sinking speed, rate of descent, descent rate, vertical velocity | 2 |
| the energy management of an unpowered approach | energy management, energy height, energy state, terminal area energy | 37 |
| the float after the flare | float, floating, floats together with landing, flare, touchdown | 0 |
| the span efficiency of a low aspect ratio shape | oswald, span efficiency, efficiency factor, induced drag factor | 2 |
| the drag of an ablated or roughened heat shield | ablated, ablative, ablation, roughness, roughened together with drag, lift to drag | 3 |

**The flare is studied mostly as a control and piloting task.** Of the 37 titles that name it, 11 concern automatic flare, flare control laws or guidance, and most of the rest concern piloted technique, displays and visual cues. Two relate the flare to the lift-to-drag ratio, a 1949 analysis of lift-drag ratio and stalling speed and a 1968 study of flare requirements for glide vehicles of low lift-to-drag ratio, and they are the nearest the literature comes to the corridor derived here from energy.

**The forebody and base drag trade is the article's own analysis.** Two titles name the forebody together with the base or the afterbody, so the factor of three at the optimum rests on Hoerner's relation and on Saltzman, Wang and Iliff's flight data rather than on a literature of the trade.

**The sink rate at touchdown is almost never the subject of a title**, which agrees with Larson's statement that the lifting bodies' vertical velocity at touchdown was not instrumented. Two titles carry the terms.

**Energy management is a reentry and orbiter subject.** Of the 37 titles that name it, 19 concern the Shuttle, a reusable or entry vehicle, a boost-glide vehicle or an unpowered glide.

**The float, the span efficiency of a lifting body and the drag of a roughened heat shield have almost no titles of their own**, so the float after a 1.5 g flare, the Oswald factor of 0.6 and the roughness penalty at landing rest on the documents cited where they are derived.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** A record that shares a word with the subject and nothing else is excluded.

**The vocabulary of this subject belongs to other fields more than to aeronautics, and three cases are severe.** Flare is overwhelmingly the solar flare, and secondarily the gas flare and the flare stack of petrochemical engineering. Energy management belongs to power grids, buildings and batteries, and in the report archives it names, among much else, a manual on energy conservation in Navy family housing. Base is the air base, the database and the base station, and survives here only because base drag carries its own disambiguating word.

**Much of the Space Shuttle's literature is not about flying it.** Titles naming the Shuttle or its orbiter also cover communications, payload experiments, launch-site operations, waste handling and materials, and only those on its aerodynamics, entry, approach, landing and handling are admitted. Approach, landing and terminal area also name air traffic scheduling and airspace operations, lifting-surface theory also names turbomachinery cascades, and drag also names ships, hydrofoils, ordnance and spheres in creeping flow, and these are excluded.

**Other records that share a word with the subject and nothing else are excluded as well.** They include multi-criteria decision studies that match approach and criteria, combustion studies of flames held behind bluff bodies, road and ground vehicle dynamics, economics and management papers including three on an economic hard landing, particle and Stokes-flow mechanics, marine and ocean engineering, space plasma and planetary papers with no landing in them, energy and chemistry papers, studies of landing in sport and human biomechanics, medical simulators, pyrotechnic illumination flares, solar flares, and studies of pigeons, honeybees, a cormorant and insect flight. Correction, erratum, clarification, retraction and withdrawal notices, figure, table and supplementary-material records, peer-review reports and journal front matter are also excluded, because a survey counts research works and these are parts of works or editorial events. Book reviews, dictionary and other short reference entries, news items and meeting notices are excluded for the same reason, and so is a second deposit of a document already counted, such as an abstract-journal or reprint listing, a preprint or a set of presentation slides beside the paper itself.

**Three families that a shared exclusion list refuses elsewhere are admitted here because they are this subject**, namely hypersonic and reentry vehicles, because a lifting body is an entry shape, head-up displays for the approach, which belong to the handling qualities literature, and road vehicle drag, which is where the base-drag physics now lives.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept, 121 in all.** Boattails of artillery shells and bullets are kept because a projectile base is a blunt base. Cylinder and bluff-body wakes from wind engineering are kept for the wake physics, rotorcraft stability and the handling qualities of spacecraft docking for their methods, and a study of body and feather drag in a peregrine falcon for its drag measurement. A reader may weigh each accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, as reported by the accessible record.** The X-24A flew 28 times between 17 April 1969 and 4 June 1971, 18 of them under power, reaching Mach 1.60 and 71,400 feet. It was rebuilt as the X-24B, which flew 36 times between 1 August 1973 and 26 November 1975, 24 of them under power, reaching Mach 1.752, or 1,164 miles an hour, and 74,100 feet. These figures are from the flight log printed by Reed. On 5 and 20 August 1975 John Manke and Michael Love landed the X-24B on the main concrete runway at Edwards, Manke at a planned mark 5,000 feet along it. The approach technique, a flare of about 1.5 g from 1,000 feet to level flight at 100 feet followed by a float, is documented by Dana and Gentry for the lifting bodies of 1970, and the Flight Research Center's case for flying an orbiter unpowered was published in the same year. The X-24A is the vehicle for which X-23A was requested in November 1965 and refused in December, and which received X-24A in 1967.

**Flight-determined data taken from a published source.** The dimensions, wetted areas, base areas and weights in the vehicle table are from Saltzman, Wang and Iliff, as is the finding that full-scale base drag requires a Hoerner coefficient near 0.10 against the model-scale 0.029, the pair of optimum coefficients 0.1284 and 0.3852, and the measured tailcone-on lift-to-drag ratio of 7.5 for the Enterprise. The flight-measured maximum lift-to-drag ratios by trim are from the same authors' 2002 assessment. The X-24A's touchdown airspeeds, impact load factors and miss distances are from Larson's tables, and the means and spreads quoted for them are computed here from those tables. The X-24B's derivative comparison is Sim's.

**Engineering analysis, performed here and checkable.** The drag bucket and its differentiation, the result that total drag is three times forebody drag at the optimum, the cancellation of reference area from the lift-to-drag expression, the predicted lift-to-drag ratios for all seven vehicles, the square-root-of-three tailcone prediction, the approach angle and sink rate, the integrated flare, the load factor solved from the quoted touchdown speed, the corridor bounds, the energy accounting, the float after a 1.5 g flare, the matched comparison with the flight-measured lift-to-drag ratios, the thrust a shallower glide slope would need, the effect of ablated roughness, and the statistics computed from Larson's landing tables are all derived in this article from stated assumptions or cited tables.

**Inference, and flagged as such.** That the X-24B approached in a high-base-area trim is inferred from the fact that the resulting lift-to-drag ratio reproduces the documented flare height at the documented load factor, not from a stated flap setting, and the documented landing configuration of the X-24A had its upper flaps closed, with speed brakes available. The 1.19 g solved from the quoted touchdown speed describes a flare ended on the runway, which the documented technique contradicts, so it is retained as a property of the model and not as a statement of what was flown. That the X-24B's concrete landings followed the documented 1970 technique is inferred from its being the programme's pattern, not stated for those flights. That the two concrete landings caused the deletion of the orbiter's air-breathing engines follows a programme retrospective and is not established from the decision record.

**Assumptions that everything downstream inherits.** The Oswald efficiency factor of 0.6 is taken from the source's comparison curve. The flare load factor is not chosen but solved from the quoted touchdown speed, and the table shows what other choices give. The approach speed of 300 miles an hour is assumed and lies below the documented band of 270 to 300 knots indicated. The drag polar is parabolic, the flare is flown at constant load factor, and the vehicle is a point mass throughout.

**What the record does not settle.** The actual trim and base area on the X-24B's approaches, and its final-approach speed. The actual load factor flown in its flare. The touchdown speeds and miss distances of the two concrete landings, which are not in the documents read here, and touchdown sink rates for any of the lifting bodies, which Larson states were not instrumented. The base pressures below Mach 0.8, which Saltzman, Wang and Iliff estimated rather than measured. The growth in span from the X-24A to the X-24B, on which the histories and the flight-determined table disagree. The date of the decision to delete the orbiter's air-breathing engines, and so the weight of the X-24B's landings in it relative to the case the Flight Research Center had made in 1970. Several Air Force Flight Test Center reports, among them the X-24B flight planning and conduct report and the flight test and wind tunnel performance comparisons for both vehicles, were not retrievable from the Defense Technical Information Center for this article.

## Out of Scope

The detailed stability and control derivatives of both vehicles beyond the comparisons summarised here. The M2 and HL-10 programmes, which have their own histories and are covered in [Jenkins, Landis and Miller][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003]. The XLR-11 engine, which the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1] article covers. The Space Shuttle Approach and Landing Tests as a programme. Lifting-body structural design and the structural detail of the rebuild that turned the A into the B. The full decision record on the orbiter's air-breathing engines.

## Conclusion

**A blunt base costs a factor of the square root of three in lift-to-drag ratio, and everything difficult about landing an X-24 follows from that one number.**

Three instead of five means an eighteen-degree glide instead of eleven. It means approaching sixty percent faster than best glide, on purpose, because the flare needs the energy. It means beginning that flare a thousand feet up rather than thirty, and it means a corridor a few tenths of a g wide with running out of speed on one side and floating off the far end of the runway on the other.

**The X-24B flew through the middle of that corridor onto fifteen thousand feet of concrete, twice, and an orbiter that had been designed with jet engines for its landing approach flew without them.**
## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 72 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 72, 37 are established and 35 are bespoke.
Quantities are in United States customary units, with lengths in feet, speeds in feet per second, miles an hour or knots as each line states and weights in pounds, drag coefficients are referred to wetted area, reference area or base area as each line states, and the efficiency factor of 0.6, the approach speed of 300 miles an hour and the maximum lift coefficient of 0.7 are values the article assumes.

**Equation 1, Cost of the Rebuild Relative to a New Vehicle.**
The documented rebuild cost of 1.1 million dollars against an estimated 5 million for a new vehicle is a ratio of about one fifth.

$$
\frac{1.1}{5.0} = 0.22
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Growth in Length and Span from the Rebuild.**
The flight-determined table gives the X-24B 13.0 feet more length and 5.51 feet more span than the X-24A.

$$
\Delta\ell = 37.50 - 24.50 = 13.0\ \text{ft}, \qquad \Delta b = 19.14 - 13.63 = 5.51\ \text{ft}
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Propellant Fraction of the X-24A.**
The documented 5,500 pounds of propellants and gases against a launch weight of about 12,000 pounds is a propellant fraction of 0.46.
[Cochrane and Graham][ref_cochrane_graham_1971]

$$
\frac{m_p}{m_0} = \frac{5{,}500}{12{,}000} = 0.46
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Thrust Ratio of the Uprated Engine.**
The uprated LR-11 rating of 9,800 pounds against the original 8,480 pounds is a thrust increase of sixteen percent.

$$
\frac{T_B}{T_A} = \frac{9{,}800}{8{,}480} = 1.16
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Base Drag Coefficient on Wetted Area.**
The suction on a blunt base contributes a drag coefficient equal to the negative base pressure coefficient times the ratio of base area to wetted area.

$$
C_{D_b} = -C_{p_b}\,\frac{A_b}{A_w}
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Hoerner Base Pressure Correlation.**
Hoerner's correlation makes the base pressure coefficient inversely proportional to the square root of the forebody drag coefficient referred to the base area.
[Hoerner's compendium of drag data][book_hoerner_1965]
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
C_{p_b} = -\frac{K}{\sqrt{C_{D_\text{fore}}}}
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Full-Scale Value of the Hoerner Coefficient.**
Flight measurements on the X-15, the M2-F3 and the Space Shuttle require a coefficient of 0.090 to 0.100 in the Hoerner correlation.
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
K = 0.090 \ \text{to}\ 0.100
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Ratio of Full-Scale to Model Hoerner Coefficients.**
The full-scale coefficient of 0.100 is about three and a half times the model-scale value of 0.029.

$$
\frac{0.100}{0.029} = 3.4
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Reynolds Number.**
The Reynolds number is the product of speed and length divided by the kinematic viscosity.

$$
Re = \frac{V\ell}{\nu}
\tag{9}
$$

*Equation 10, Bespoke Reynolds Number Ratio of Flight to a Small Model.*
The approach Reynolds number of the X-24B is about forty times that of a model the article takes as one-twentieth scale in a tunnel at 200 feet per second.

$$
\frac{Re_\text{flight}}{Re_\text{model}} = 41
\tag{10}
$$

*Equation 11, Bespoke True Airspeed at the Middle of the Approach Band.*
The true airspeed follows from the indicated airspeed and the density ratio at Edwards, evaluated at 285 knots, the midpoint of the documented band of 270 to 300 knots.
[Falarski and Mort][ref_falarski_mort_1970]
[Dana and Gentry 1970][research_william_h_dana_j_r_gentry_1970]

$$
V = \frac{V_i}{\sqrt{\sigma}} = \frac{285 \times 1.688}{\sqrt{0.934}} = 498\ \text{ft/s}
\tag{11}
$$

*Equation 12, Bespoke Reynolds Number of the X-24A at the Middle of the Approach Band.*
At the midpoint approach speed the X-24A's flight Reynolds number on its length is about twice that of the full-scale tunnel test.

$$
Re_\text{X-24A} = 7.2\times 10^7, \qquad \frac{7.2\times 10^7}{3.24\times 10^7} = 2.2
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Equivalent Skin-Friction Coefficient.**
The equivalent skin-friction coefficient is the minimum drag coefficient referred to wetted area rather than to a reference area.

$$
C_{F_e} = C_{D_\text{min}}\,\frac{S}{A_w}
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Forebody Drag Referred to the Base Area.**
The forebody drag coefficient that the Hoerner correlation needs is the forebody equivalent skin-friction coefficient scaled by the ratio of wetted to base area.

$$
C_{D_\text{fore},b} = C_{F_e,\text{fore}}\,\frac{A_w}{A_b}
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Forebody and Base Drag Trade on Wetted Area.**
Writing both drag terms on wetted area gives a total that rises with the forebody contribution and falls through the base term, a trade the source analyses.
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
C_{F_e} = x + \frac{k\, r^{3/2}}{\sqrt{x}}
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Stationarity Condition of the Drag Trade.**
Setting the derivative of the total with respect to the forebody contribution to zero gives the condition for an interior minimum.

$$
\frac{dC_{F_e}}{dx} = 1 - \frac{k\,r^{3/2}}{2x^{3/2}} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad k\,r^{3/2} = 2x^{3/2}
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Optimum Forebody Contribution.**
The minimum lies at a forebody contribution proportional to the base-to-wetted area ratio, with a coefficient set by the Hoerner coefficient and profile factor.

$$
x_\text{opt} = \left(\frac{k}{2}\right)^{2/3} r
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Total Drag at the Optimum as Three Times the Forebody Drag.**
Substituting the optimum back makes the total exactly three times the forebody contribution, independent of every parameter in the trade.
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
C_{F_e} = x + \frac{2x^{3/2}}{\sqrt{x}} = x + 2x = 3x
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Ratio of the Source's Optimum Coefficients.**
The source's minimum total coefficient of $0.3852\,r$ is exactly three times its optimal forebody coefficient of $0.1284\,r$.
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
\frac{0.3852}{0.1284} = 3.000
\tag{19}
$$

*Equation 20, Bespoke Optimum Forebody Coefficient in the Article's Arrangement.*
Applying the full-scale Hoerner coefficient of 0.10 with a profile factor of 0.92 in the article's arrangement gives 0.1435, twelve percent above the source's value.

$$
\left(\frac{0.10/0.92}{2}\right)^{2/3} = 0.1435
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Maximum Lift-to-Drag Ratio of a Parabolic Polar.**
For a parabolic polar the maximum lift-to-drag ratio is half the square root of pi times efficiency factor times aspect ratio over the parasite drag coefficient.

$$
\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{max} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi e A}{C_{D_0}}}
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Maximum Lift-to-Drag Ratio in Wetted Area Form.**
Expressing the parasite drag on wetted area and the aspect ratio through the span makes the reference area cancel, leaving span squared over wetted area as the governing variable.
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{max} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi e\, b^2}{A_w\, C_{F_e}}}
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Aspect Ratio and Wetted Aspect Ratio.**
The aspect ratio is span squared over reference area and the wetted aspect ratio is span squared over wetted area.
[Saltzman et al. 2007][research_saltzman_2007]

$$
A = \frac{b^2}{S}, \qquad A_\text{wetted} = \frac{b^2}{A_w}
\tag{23}
$$

*Equation 24, Bespoke Lift-to-Drag Gain from Covering the Base.*
Within the article's base drag model, removing the base term cuts the drag to one third, so the lift-to-drag ratio rises by the square root of three.

$$
\frac{(L/D)_\text{tailcone}}{(L/D)_\text{truncated}} = \sqrt{3} = 1.73
\tag{24}
$$

*Equation 25, Bespoke Predicted Lift-to-Drag Ratio of Enterprise with the Tailcone.*
The truncated Enterprise value scaled by the square root of three predicts 7.05, six percent below the measured 7.5.

$$
\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{tailcone} = 7.05
\tag{25}
$$

*Equation 26, Bespoke Parabolic Drag Polar of the X-24B.*
The drag polar of the X-24B uses an induced drag factor of 0.479 that follows from an efficiency factor the article assumes as 0.6.

$$
C_D = C_{D_0} + k_i C_L^2, \qquad k_i = \frac{1}{\pi e A} = 0.479
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Lift Coefficient in Level Flight and Dynamic Pressure.**
The lift coefficient that balances the weight is the weight over dynamic pressure times reference area, with dynamic pressure half the density times the square of speed.

$$
C_L = \frac{W}{q S}, \qquad q = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2
\tag{27}
$$

*Equation 28, Bespoke Best Glide Condition of the X-24B.*
Equating the parasite and induced terms of the assumed polar gives a best-glide lift coefficient of 0.30 and a maximum lift-to-drag ratio of 3.43.

$$
C_L^* = \sqrt{\frac{C_{D_0}}{k_i}} = 0.304, \qquad \left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{max} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{C_{D_0} k_i}} = 3.43
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Best Glide Angle.*
The best glide angle is the inverse tangent of the reciprocal of the maximum lift-to-drag ratio of the assumed polar, about 16 degrees.

$$
\gamma^* = \arctan\frac{1}{(L/D)_\text{max}} = 16.2^\circ
\tag{29}
$$

*Equation 30, Bespoke Best Glide Speed.*
The lift balance at the best-glide lift coefficient and the density taken for Edwards gives about 188 miles an hour.
[Edwards Air Force Base][ref_edwards_afb]

$$
V^* = \sqrt{\frac{2W}{\rho S C_L^*}} = 276\ \text{ft/s} = 188\ \text{mph}
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Approach Speed Relative to Best Glide.*
The approach speed of 300 miles an hour that the article assumes is 1.60 times the best-glide speed.

$$
\frac{V}{V^*} = 1.60
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Lift Coefficient at the Assumed Approach Speed.*
Because the lift coefficient falls as the inverse square of speed, the assumed approach speed brings it to 0.39 of the best-glide value.

$$
\frac{C_L}{C_L^*} = \left(\frac{V}{V^*}\right)^{-2} = 0.39
\tag{32}
$$

*Equation 33, Bespoke Induced Share of the Approach Drag.*
At the assumed approach speed the induced term is about one eighth of the total drag of the assumed polar.

$$
\frac{k_i C_L^2}{C_D} = 0.13
\tag{33}
$$

*Equation 34, Bespoke Approach Path Angle.*
The lift-to-drag ratio of 2.34 at the assumed approach speed gives a path angle of about 23 degrees.

$$
\gamma = \arctan\frac{1}{2.34} = 23.2^\circ
\tag{34}
$$

*Equation 35, Bespoke Approach Sink Rate.*
The vertical component of the assumed approach speed on that path is about 10,400 feet per minute.

$$
\dot h = V\sin\gamma = 173\ \text{ft/s} = 10{,}400\ \text{ft/min}
\tag{35}
$$

*Equation 36, Bespoke Sink Rate of a Transport Approach.*
A transport on a three-degree approach at 140 knots, values the article takes as representative, descends at about 740 feet per minute.

$$
\dot h = 140 \times 1.688 \times \sin 3^\circ \times 60 = 742\ \text{ft/min}
\tag{36}
$$

*Equation 37, Bespoke Ratio of Lifting Body to Transport Sink Rate.*
The modelled lifting-body sink rate is about fourteen times the representative transport value.

$$
\frac{10{,}400}{742} = 14
\tag{37}
$$

*Equation 38, Bespoke Documented Approach Band Relative to Best Glide.*
The documented band of 321 to 357 miles an hour true is 1.71 to 1.90 times the best-glide speed of the assumed polar.
[Dana and Gentry 1970][research_william_h_dana_j_r_gentry_1970]

$$
\frac{321}{188} = 1.71 \quad \text{to} \quad \frac{357}{188} = 1.90
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Radius of a Pull-Up at Constant Load Factor.**
A path curving at load factor $n$ in a vertical plane has an instantaneous radius of speed squared over gravity times $n$ minus one.

$$
R = \frac{V^2}{g(n-1)}
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Arc Length per Unit Path Angle.**
The distance along the path per unit change of path angle is the negative of the instantaneous radius.

$$
\frac{ds}{d\gamma} = -R = -\frac{V^2}{g(n-1)}
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Height and Horizontal Distance Along the Path.**
Height and horizontal distance change along the path as the sine and cosine of the path angle.

$$
\frac{dh}{ds} = \sin\gamma, \qquad \frac{dx}{ds} = \cos\gamma
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, Speed Change Along the Path.**
Along the path the speed changes with the difference between the weight component along the path and the drag, divided by mass times speed.

$$
\frac{dV}{ds} = \frac{W\sin\gamma - D}{mV}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Lift Coefficient and Drag at Load Factor.**
The lift coefficient the load factor demands and the drag from the parabolic polar at that lift coefficient close the flare equations.

$$
C_L = \frac{nW}{qS}, \qquad D = qS\left(C_{D_0} + k_i C_L^2\right)
\tag{43}
$$

**Equation 44, Load Factor.**
The load factor is the ratio of lift to weight.

$$
n = \frac{L}{W}
\tag{44}
$$

*Equation 45, Bespoke Load Factor Solved for the Quoted Touchdown Speed.*
Integrating the flare from the assumed 300 miles an hour and adjusting the load factor until touchdown at the quoted 200 miles an hour gives 1.19 g, a flare from about 2,160 feet lasting about 22 seconds.

$$
n = 1.19, \qquad h_\text{flare} = 2{,}163\ \text{ft}, \qquad t = 21.9\ \text{s}
\tag{45}
$$

*Equation 46, Bespoke Flare Compared with a Transport Flare.*
Against a transport flare the article takes to begin at about thirty feet and last about three seconds, the modelled flare starts about seventy times higher and lasts about seven times longer.

$$
\frac{2{,}163}{30} = 72, \qquad \frac{21.9}{3} = 7.3
\tag{46}
$$

*Equation 47, Bespoke Flare Distance as a Fraction of the Runway.*
The horizontal projection of the modelled flare covers about 62 percent of the 15,000 foot concrete runway.

$$
\frac{9{,}306}{15{,}000} = 0.62
\tag{47}
$$

*Equation 48, Bespoke Lift Coefficient at the Start of the Flare.*
The solved load factor times the approach lift coefficient gives a flare lift coefficient of about 0.14.

$$
C_L = \frac{nW}{qS} = 1.19 \times 0.120 = 0.142
\tag{48}
$$

*Equation 49, Bespoke Touchdown Speed Gain from Pulling Harder.*
In the flare model raising the load factor from 2 to 3 g lowers the touchdown speed by only 4 miles an hour.

$$
V_\text{td}(3g) - V_\text{td}(2g) = 260 - 256 = 4\ \text{mph}
\tag{49}
$$

*Equation 50, Bespoke Stall Speed.*
The stall speed at the lift and drag test weight with a maximum usable lift coefficient the article assumes as 0.7 is about 124 miles an hour.

$$
V_\text{stall} = \sqrt{\frac{2W}{\rho S C_{L_\text{max}}}} = 124\ \text{mph}
\tag{50}
$$

*Equation 51, Bespoke Touchdown Speed Margin over Stall.*
The modelled touchdown speed at 1.19 g is 1.60 times the stall speed of the assumed maximum lift coefficient.

$$
\frac{V_\text{td}}{V_\text{stall}} = \frac{199}{124} = 1.60
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Height Span of the Documented Flare.**
The documented flare from 1,000 feet to the 100 foot level-off spans 900 feet of height.

$$
h_\text{flare} = 1{,}000 - 100 = 900\ \text{ft}
\tag{52}
$$

*Equation 53, Bespoke Float Distance after the Flare.*
Holding level flight at one g, the article writes the float distance as the speed decay that the polar sets plus a term for the level-off height times a mean lift-to-drag ratio.

$$
\frac{dV}{ds} = -\frac{g}{V\,(L/D)}, \qquad s_\text{float} = \frac{1}{g}\int_{V_\text{td}}^{V_1} V\,\frac{L}{D}\,dV + h_1\,\overline{\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)}
\tag{53}
$$

*Equation 54, Bespoke Float Distance, Mean Lift-to-Drag Ratio and Duration.*
Decelerating from 241 to 200 miles an hour on the assumed polar gives a float of about 2,300 feet lasting about seven seconds.

$$
s_\text{float} = 2{,}303\ \text{ft}, \qquad \overline{L/D} = 3.25, \qquad t \approx 7.1\ \text{s}
\tag{54}
$$

**Equation 55, Sink Rate at a Residual Path Angle.**
The sink rate is the speed times the sine of the path angle, reported at a small residual angle because the flare drives the angle to zero.

$$
\dot h = V\sin\gamma_\text{residual}
\tag{55}
$$

**Equation 56, Mean Impact Load Factor of the X-24A.**
The mean of the 25 peak normal accelerations at ground impact in Larson's table for the X-24A is 1.43 g.
[Larson][research_larson_1972]

$$
\bar n_\text{impact} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i = 1.43, \qquad N = 25
\tag{56}
$$

*Equation 57, Bespoke Energy Height at the Start of the Flare.*
The modelled flare height plus the kinetic energy height of the assumed approach speed gives a total energy height of about 5,170 feet.

$$
h_E = h + \frac{V^2}{2g} = 2{,}163 + 3{,}009 = 5{,}172\ \text{ft}
\tag{57}
$$

*Equation 58, Bespoke Energy Height at Touchdown.*
At zero height and the touchdown speed of 199 miles an hour that the flare model reaches, close to the quoted 200, the energy height is about 1,320 feet.

$$
h_{E,\text{td}} = \frac{V_\text{td}^2}{2g} = 1{,}322\ \text{ft}
\tag{58}
$$

*Equation 59, Bespoke Share of Energy Spent in the Flare.*
The difference of the modelled and touchdown energy heights is about 74 percent of the energy at the start of the flare.

$$
\frac{5{,}172 - 1{,}322}{5{,}172} = 0.74
\tag{59}
$$

*Equation 60, Bespoke Mean Deceleration Along the Flare.*
The change in squared speed over twice the modelled arc length gives a mean deceleration of about 0.18 g.

$$
\bar a = \frac{V_i^2 - V_f^2}{2 s} = 0.18\,g
\tag{60}
$$

*Equation 61, Bespoke Lift-to-Drag Ratios of the X-24A and X-24B.*
The article's polar with full base drag and the assumed efficiency factor gives 2.99 and 3.43, a ratio of 1.15.
[Reed][book_reed_1997]

$$
\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{X-24A} = 2.99, \qquad \left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{X-24B} = 3.43, \qquad \text{ratio} = 1.15
\tag{61}
$$

**Equation 62, Lift-to-Drag Gain from the Wetted Aspect Ratio.**
Because the maximum lift-to-drag ratio goes as the square root of the wetted aspect ratio, a rise of 1.23 in that ratio accounts for a factor of 1.11.

$$
\sqrt{1.23} = 1.11
\tag{62}
$$

**Equation 63, Glide Radius from Height.**
A glide at a fixed lift-to-drag ratio reaches a horizontal radius equal to the starting height times that ratio.
[Bell 1964][research_bell_1964]
[Kelley et al. 1982][research_kelley_1982]
[Knapp and Barton 1968][research_knapp_barton_1968]
[Sleeman 1971][research_sleeman_1971]

$$
r = h\,\frac{L}{D}
\tag{63}
$$

**Equation 64, Ratio of Powered-Approach Runway to Concrete Runway.**
The 7.5 miles the HL-10's powered approaches needed is 2.6 times the 15,000 feet of concrete at Edwards.
[Kock and Fulton][research_berwin_m_kock_fitzhugh_l_fulton_1970]
[Reed][book_reed_1997]

$$
\frac{7.5 \times 5{,}280}{15{,}000} = \frac{39{,}600}{15{,}000} = 2.6
\tag{64}
$$

**Equation 65, Statistics of the X-24A Longitudinal Miss Distances.**
The signed mean, mean absolute value and sample standard deviation of 20 measured X-24A touchdown misses are about 1,130, 1,450 and 1,680 feet.
[Larson][research_larson_1972]

$$
\bar x = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i = 1{,}125\ \text{ft}, \qquad \overline{|x|} = 1{,}450\ \text{ft}, \qquad s_x = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{N-1}} = 1{,}678\ \text{ft}
\tag{65}
$$

**Equation 66, Probability of Landing within 500 Feet under the Lakebed Fit.**
Under Larson's normal fit with a mean 112 feet short and a standard deviation of 1,793.6 feet, about 22 percent of landings fall within 500 feet of the aim point.
[Larson][research_larson_1972]

$$
P(|x| \le 500) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{500-\mu}{\sigma_x}\right) - \Phi\!\left(\frac{-500-\mu}{\sigma_x}\right) = 0.22
\tag{66}
$$

**Equation 67, Ratio of Lakebed Scatter to the Expected Accuracy.**
The lakebed standard deviation is about 3.6 times the 500 foot accuracy expected on the concrete.

$$
\frac{\sigma_x}{500} = 3.6
\tag{67}
$$

*Equation 68, Bespoke Departures of the Model from Flight-Determined Ratios.*
The article's lift-to-drag ratios differ from the flight-determined values matched by base area by $+3$, $-9$ and $+8$ percent.
[Saltzman et al. 2002][research_saltzman_2002]

$$
\frac{4.39}{4.25} - 1 = +3\%, \qquad \frac{2.99}{3.28} - 1 = -9\%, \qquad \frac{4.88}{4.50} - 1 = +8\%
\tag{68}
$$

**Equation 69, Thrust to Change the Path Angle at Constant Speed.**
Holding the speed while changing the path angle needs a thrust equal to the change in the weight component along the path.
[Kock and Fulton][research_berwin_m_kock_fitzhugh_l_fulton_1970]

$$
T = W\left(\sin\gamma_1 - \sin\gamma_2\right)
\tag{69}
$$

*Equation 70, Bespoke Thrust for a Six Degree Powered Approach.*
Shallowing the modelled 23.2 degree approach of the X-24B to 6 degrees needs about 2,460 pounds of thrust, 29 percent of its weight.

$$
T = 8{,}500\left(\sin 23.2^\circ - \sin 6^\circ\right) = 2{,}460\ \text{lb}
\tag{70}
$$

**Equation 71, Lift-to-Drag Ratio with Roughness Drag.**
At a given lift the lift-to-drag ratio falls in proportion to the drag, so a fractional drag increase divides it by one plus that fraction.
[Reed][book_reed_1997]

$$
\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{rough} = \frac{L/D}{1 + \Delta C_D/C_D}
\tag{71}
$$

*Equation 72, Bespoke Touchdown Speed as a Function of Aerodynamics Alone.*
The article writes the touchdown speed of its flare model as a function of load factor, wing loading, polar coefficients and density alone, with no term for the pilot.

$$
V_\text{td} = F\left(n,\ \frac{W}{S},\ C_{D_0},\ k_i,\ \rho\right)
\tag{72}
$$

### Notation

- $C_{D_b}$, the base drag coefficient referred to wetted area
- $C_{p_b}$, the base pressure coefficient
- $A_b$, the base area
- $A_w$, the wetted area
- $K$, the coefficient of the Hoerner base pressure correlation
- $Re$, the Reynolds number
- $\nu$, the kinematic viscosity
- $\sigma$, the ratio of air density to sea-level density
- $V_i$, the indicated airspeed, and in Equation 60 the speed at the start of the flare
- $C_{F_e}$, the equivalent skin-friction coefficient referred to wetted area
- $r$, the ratio of base area to wetted area, and in Equation 63 the glide radius
- $x$, the forebody contribution to the equivalent skin-friction coefficient, and in Equations 41 and 65 a horizontal distance
- $e$, the efficiency factor, taken as 0.6
- $A$, the aspect ratio
- $b$, the span
- $S$, the reference area
- $C_{D_0}$, the parasite drag coefficient
- $k_i$, the induced drag factor
- $C_L^*$, the lift coefficient at best glide, with $V^*$ the best-glide speed
- $\gamma$, the flight path angle
- $n$, the load factor
- $R$, the instantaneous radius of the flare
- $s$, the distance along the path
- $V_\text{td}$, the touchdown speed
- $C_{L_\text{max}}$, the maximum usable lift coefficient, taken as 0.7
- $h_E$, the energy height
- $\sigma_x$, the standard deviation of the touchdown miss distance in Larson's fit
- $\Phi$, the standard normal distribution function
